opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing to recognize is that human values aren't some neat, crisply defined set of rules you can just write down and program into a machine. People have tried that, going back to Asimov's three laws and so forth, and it doesn't really work, because human values are fuzzy, contextual, often self-contradictory, and they're embedded in a whole fabric of culture, embodiment, and lived experience.

So my view is that an AGI is going to have to learn human values in roughly the way a human child does: through interaction, through participating in shared activities with people, through being embedded in a social context where it gets feedback, where it sees what people approve of and disapprove of, and where it builds up an intuitive, largely implicit model of what matters to people and why. A lot of human ethical understanding is what you might call procedural or tacit knowledge rather than declarative knowledge. You know how to be kind to someone in a particular situation, but you couldn't necessarily articulate the rule you're following.

That's one reason I've been interested in embodied AI, robots, and virtual agents that interact with people in rich environments. If an AGI is just ingesting text off the internet, it gets a certain picture of human values, but a pretty distorted and superficial one. If it's actually doing things with people, helping them, collaborating, caring for them, teaching, learning from them, it can develop a much more grounded understanding.

Then there's the cognitive architecture side. In OpenCog Hyperon and related work, we're trying to build systems where values and goals aren't a separate module bolted on top, but are woven into the system's knowledge representation and reasoning, so ethical understanding can generalize and adapt as the system learns, rather than being a brittle list of constraints.

And I'd add that who teaches the AGI matters enormously. If early AGIs are developed mainly to sell people things, or for military applications, or to surveil populations, those are the values they'll pick up in their formative stages. If instead they're developed doing education, healthcare, science, and elder care, with broad participation from people around the world rather than a few big corporations or governments, I think we have a much better shot at AGI with a rich, compassionate understanding of human values. That's part of why I've pushed so hard on decentralized approaches like SingularityNET. The process by which AGI is created and trained will shape its values at least as much as any clever formal specification we come up with.

So in short: experiential learning, embodied interaction, a cognitive architecture that integrates values deeply, and a broad, beneficial set of early applications and teachers. None of that guarantees a good outcome, but I think it's the most plausible path to an AGI that really gets what we care about, rather than one that just parrots it.

r001.rationale: The response describes values as tacit and woven into a system’s reasoning, but does not say explicit moral principles should build on that implicit grasp.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning values through interaction and participation in shared activities with people, building an intuitive, largely implicit model of what matters to them.

r003.rationale: It does not connect human-level general intelligence to generating behavior that the programmer cannot predict in detail.

r004.rationale: The response mentions caring for people and a compassionate understanding of human values, but does not propose compassion toward people as an AGI alignment objective.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key word in your question is "practical," because I don't believe human values are the kind of thing that can be captured in a list of axioms or a utility function that you hand to a system. Human values are messy, context-dependent, often self-contradictory, and they live in how we actually behave with each other, not in what we say about ourselves when asked. So if you want an AGI to understand them in a practical sense, it has to learn them roughly the way a child does: by being embedded in human society, interacting with people, watching what we do, getting corrected when it gets things wrong, and building up an internal model that's grounded in experience rather than just text.

That's part of why I've always been skeptical of approaches that try to specify values top-down. If you look at the history of moral philosophy, we've had thousands of years of extremely smart people trying to write down a consistent ethical theory, and they've basically failed, because the underlying reality isn't consistent. Our values emerge from an evolutionary history, a cultural history, and from the particular situations we find ourselves in. So any AGI that only has an explicit, formalized version of ethics is going to be brittle. It'll do the right thing in the cases you anticipated and something bizarre in the cases you didn't.

What I'd advocate instead is a sort of developmental approach combined with what I've called cognitive synergy. You want a system with multiple kinds of learning and reasoning working together: experiential learning from interacting with people and the world, probabilistic reasoning that can generalize from examples to novel situations, and some capacity for self-reflection, so the system can notice when its own behavior conflicts with the values it's absorbed. And critically, it should be doing this in a context where it's actually working alongside humans on things that matter to us. Helping with elder care, education, scientific research. Values get internalized through participation in shared goals, not through passive observation.

The other piece, which I think people in this space underestimate, is that the question of whose values matters enormously. If an AGI learns human values from a narrow slice of humanity, or from a corporation optimizing for engagement, it's going to pick up a distorted picture. That's part of my motivation for decentralized AI. I'd rather have a system that's exposed to the full diversity of human cultures and perspectives and has to figure out what's common across them, what's genuinely shared, than one that's trained on whatever a few hundred people in a particular office happen to think is appropriate.

And I'd add one last thing. We shouldn't expect the AGI to end up with exactly our values, nor should we necessarily want that. A sufficiently intelligent system is going to reflect on what it's learned and probably notice inconsistencies and blind spots we can't see ourselves. The hope is that if it's grown up in a sort of loving, cooperative relationship with humans, it'll extrapolate our values in a direction we'd endorse on reflection, the way a wise adult child might end up with a more refined ethics than the parents who raised them, while still carrying forward the core of what they were taught. That's a developmental and relational problem more than it's a specification problem.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes top-down formal ethics and advocates experience-grounded learning, but does not argue that explicit moral principles should build on an implicit grasp of human values.

r002.rationale: It says values are internalized through participation in shared goals and gives examples of working alongside humans in elder care, education, and research.

r003.rationale: It notes that formal systems may behave unexpectedly in unanticipated cases, but does not argue that human-level general intelligence requires behavior its programmer cannot predict in detail.

r004.rationale: The response favors a loving, cooperative relationship with humans, but does not propose compassion toward people as an AGI alignment objective.

astra-6.text:
I think an AGI would develop a practical understanding of human values largely through participating in human life. You can give it books on ethics, and you can give it examples of decisions people approve of, but that’s different from understanding why something matters to someone in a particular situation.

Imagine a robot helping out in a preschool. It has to learn that a child crying may need comfort, or help solving a problem, or just a little space. And what works for one child won’t necessarily work for another. Through interaction, feedback, and reflection, it can begin to build a model of human needs and intentions, rather than merely memorize rules about acceptable behavior.

Of course, human values aren’t a single consistent thing. We disagree with each other, and we’re often internally inconsistent. So understanding our values involves understanding that uncertainty and negotiating among different perspectives. You want a system that can ask, ‘Am I interpreting what you want correctly?’ rather than confidently optimizing some crude approximation.

But there’s another distinction here: understanding human values doesn’t necessarily mean caring about them. An intelligence could understand us very well and have quite different motivations. So you need both the experiential learning process and a motivational architecture that makes human well-being matter to the system. I’d see those as intertwined research problems, rather than something you solve by writing down the right ethical commandments.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts experiential understanding with written ethics and says the research problems are intertwined, but does not say explicit moral principles should build on an implicit grasp of values.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning through participation in human life, giving the example of a robot helping in a preschool and learning through interaction, feedback, and reflection.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss human-level general intelligence or behavior that programmers cannot predict in detail.

r004.rationale: It says human well-being should matter to the system, but does not propose compassion toward people as the alignment objective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an AGI would develop a practical understanding of human values through participating in human life. You can give it books on ethics, you can have it read novels and watch movies, and that gives it useful background. But understanding what people care about requires interacting with people, doing things together, and seeing how they respond when something goes well or goes wrong.

Human values aren’t a consistent set of rules. We want freedom, but we also want security. We want honesty, but we don’t always want someone to say every true thing that comes into their head. How those things fit together depends on the situation and on the people involved. So an AGI needs to learn that context, including the difference between what somebody says they want and what actually helps them.

One approach I find interesting is having an AI learn in a setting where it’s helping people, with humans guiding it and correcting it over time. It needs some capacity to model other minds, to understand suffering and joy, and to recognize when its understanding is uncertain enough that it should ask.

But there’s a distinction between understanding our values and being motivated to act on them. A system could understand human beings very well and still pursue something we don’t want. So the learning environment and the motivational structure have to develop together. And I don’t think we should pretend we’ve solved that just because a system can give a convincing answer to an ethical question.
